Source for these selected fields and contracts: Material.h, MaterialInstance.h, MaterialInstance.h, MaterialShared.h, MaterialShared.h, MaterialRenderProxy.h.

Material instances reuse a parent material while changing selected parameters. Ten slabs can share one compiled surface program and use different tint values or texture bindings. A dynamic material instance lets gameplay change appropriate runtime parameters. Static switches are different: they affect which code is compiled and can create distinct shader variants. Confusing these categories leads to poor architecture. A runtime color change should not require regenerating geometry, while a change that selects a different compiled branch cannot always be represented by overwriting one float.

Material slots connect a mesh's sections to its appearance. Suppose the fountain basin has section zero for stone and section one for brass. The asset supplies default materials, while a placed component can override them. Neither arrangement requires embedding a complete material program into each vertex. Section data selects a material binding; vertex data supplies the geometric inputs that the chosen program consumes. The same brass material may appear on the gate handle and the fountain drain despite their geometry coming from different assets.

Material domains and blending choices also affect where work belongs. An opaque surface can contribute a nearest visible surface and usually write depth. A masked material either accepts or rejects a covered sample based on an opacity threshold, which is useful for leaves and fences. A translucent material requires compositing contributions through or over other surfaces. A volume-domain material describes participating matter rather than a thin boundary. A decal modifies the appearance of another surface, and a post-process material operates on image-space inputs. Treating all of these as interchangeable “materials on a triangle” would hide essential renderer contracts.

Vertex displacement crosses the boundary between appearance and geometry. Unreal's world-position-offset material logic can move vertices, such as making leaves sway. The program is authored as material behavior, but the consequences include bounds, shadows, previous positions, and ray-tracing compatibility. A material system must therefore report relevant capabilities to the geometry and pass systems. Opacity masking has a similar effect on coverage. The pass processor cannot choose a cheap opaque depth shader if the material's holes determine which samples exist.

Unreal also supports richer material representations such as Substrate, so the familiar list of base color, metallic, and roughness should be understood as an accessible starting model rather than a permanent complete schema for every shading path. The architectural requirement is broader: the renderer and material compiler agree on a surface representation, the allowed operations, and the consumers that can evaluate or store it. A modular scene system should refer to a material program and its binding data while allowing that representation to evolve. It should not hard-code the editor's node graph into every geometry provider.

12A visible surface becomes a lit pixel

At dusk, switch on the courtyard lamp. The lamp has a world position, a color, an intensity, and a spatial shape describing where it sends light. These properties belong to the light, while the stone's roughness and color belong to the surface. Keeping them separate is what lets one lamp illuminate many materials and one material respond to many lamps. In Unreal, light components create renderer-facing light state, analogous in purpose to the primitive handoff but using light-specific types. FLightSceneProxy provides rendering properties and specialized behavior for lights. The integration begins in LightComponent.cpp and LightSceneProxy.h.

The lamp has its own proxy and scene-info record
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the courtyard
FLightSceneProxy: light propertiesLightToWorld, position/color getters, light-type-specific radius/source-shape queries and shadow policy.Describe where the lamp sends light and how the renderer should handle its supported shadow behavior.
FLightSceneProxy: specialized operationsVirtual light-parameter and shadow-initializer operations supplied by concrete light types.A point light and a directional light share scene integration while producing different lighting/shadow work.
FLightSceneInfo: scene membershipProxy, Id, Scene, OctreeId, interaction-list heads and precomputed-lighting validity state.Integrate the lamp with renderer lookup and applicable light/primitive interactions. It does not store every object’s final illumination.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: LightSceneProxy.h, LightSceneInfo.h.

A directional light approximates a distant source whose incoming direction is effectively shared across the scene. A point light emits around a position. A spot light restricts emission to a cone. A rect light describes an area-shaped source with the implementation's supported approximations. A sky light represents environmental illumination rather than an ordinary local bulb. Their shadowing and performance characteristics differ. The common requirement is that the renderer can obtain the incident-light direction and contribution relevant to a surface point, then evaluate the material's response.

To make that point concrete, suppose the slab faces upward and the lamp lies above it. A diffuse response includes the cosine between the surface normal and the incoming-light direction. If the normal and direction align, the cosine factor is one; if the light grazes the slab at sixty degrees from the normal, it is one half. A rough dielectric surface also has a specular response determined by its material model. Distance attenuation and the light's intensity affect the arriving illumination. These computations evaluate lighting; sampling the moss texture evaluates the surface. A deferred renderer separates much of that work.

Rasterization first answers a geometric question: which projected triangles cover each sample? Depth testing determines which accepted surface is closest for an opaque view. Interpolation supplies values such as UVs and normals at the covered sample. The material then evaluates the visible surface's properties. In a conventional deferred path, those properties are encoded in several screen-sized render targets collectively called the GBuffer, short for geometry buffer. Depth is typically stored separately and can help reconstruct position. The buffers contain a description suitable for later lighting, not a complete copy of the original mesh.

Unreal's FGBufferData exposes a logical decoded representation with fields such as world normal, base color, metallic, roughness, shading-model identity, and other data used by supported shading paths. The actual texture packing depends on configuration and feature choices; the logical structure is not a declaration that every field occupies a separate full-precision texture. This distinction is important when extending a renderer: the surface contract and the storage encoding are related but separate designs. The decoded structure is in DeferredShadingCommon.ush.

FGBufferData: decoded surface information for one sample
InformationConcrete Unreal data or operationUse in the courtyard
Surface orientationWorldNormal and, for supported paths, other orientation data.The lighting calculation knows which way this stone sample faces.
Reflectance parametersBaseColor, Metallic, Specular and Roughness.Distinguish broad stone reflections from a smoother brass surface at the same illumination.
Model selection and extensionsShadingModelID and CustomData with model-dependent meaning.Choose how to interpret extra surface information and evaluate the supported lighting response.
Depth and ancillary dataDepth, custom-depth/stencil-related values and other decoded inputs.Locate or classify the visible sample alongside its material properties.

Source for these selected fields and contracts: DeferredShadingCommon.ush.

This is a shader-side value for a surface sample, not a persistent per-object record. It is also not a universal storage schema for every rendering mode: translucent and richer material paths can require other contracts, and decoded values need not each occupy their own GBuffer texture.

Now add a second lamp. The moss texture generally does not need to be sampled from scratch once per light in the deferred opaque lighting stage. The renderer reads the stored surface attributes, evaluates the second light, and adds its contribution. For an illustrative pixel, the first light might contribute (0.12,0.10,0.06) and the second (0.02,0.03,0.05) in linear scene-referred RGB, giving (0.14,0.13,0.11) before other illumination and processing. These are invented values to show accumulation. Lighting is not performed by multiplying already tone-mapped display colors.

The approach has costs. Multiple render targets consume memory bandwidth, and a fixed encoding limits which surface information can be retained. A one-layer nearest-surface description cannot by itself represent arbitrary stacks of transparent surfaces. Specialized shading models may need additional data or passes. The reason to use deferred shading is therefore not that it is universally simpler. It makes a particular tradeoff: spend bandwidth on a reusable description of visible surfaces, then organize lighting largely independently of the original geometry submissions.

Shadows add another visibility question. The lamp illuminates a point only if the relevant path to the source is unobstructed, subject to the chosen shadow approximation. A shadow map renders depth from a light-related view and compares the shaded point against that stored depth. Unreal also has Virtual Shadow Maps and ray-traced shadow paths under appropriate configurations. The gate can be outside the player's camera and still block light reaching a visible slab. Main-view culling must therefore not erase the gate from the persistent scene merely because it is not directly visible. Shadow consumers decide their own relevant work.

Opacity and deformation must agree across those consumers. A masked leaf casts a cutout shadow only if the shadow path evaluates its coverage correctly. A wind-deformed branch casts a convincing shadow only if the shadow geometry represents the appropriate deformation. The exact performance compromise can vary with distance or quality settings, but the system needs a declared relationship between the representations. This is another reason to keep material requirements, geometry capabilities, and scene updates explicit rather than burying them inside one main-view draw callback.

The fountain spray demonstrates the limits of one opaque surface record. A translucent droplet or smoke sprite contributes through a compositing operation that depends on what is behind it. Such work often follows separate lighting and compositing paths, with sorting and order-independent techniques available for particular cases. Hair strands and participating volumes introduce their own visibility and accumulation. Deferred decals can modify receiving surfaces through decal-specific buffers or later operations. Post-processing then consumes rendered images to implement effects such as bloom, depth of field, exposure, and tone mapping. These are consumers and transformations of scene results, not extra geometry attributes that should be copied into every primitive.

The actual Unreal frame is more involved than a straight list of “geometry, lights, transparency.” The deferred renderer interleaves preparation, shadow work, surface rendering, indirect illumination, reflections, specialized effects, and post-processing, with dependencies and optional paths. FDeferredShadingSceneRenderer::Render shows calls for the base pass, diffuse indirect lighting, lights, translucency, and hair-related lighting. Its render graph describes resource access so work can be scheduled safely. We use a simplified sequence to explain causality; the implementation is a graph of dependent work rather than a fixed textbook conveyor belt. See the base-pass scheduling, lighting work, and translucency work in DeferredShadingRenderer.cpp.

Inspect the surface separately from its illumination

To reproduce the distinction in Unreal Editor, start with a desktop deferred-rendering project, place a non-Nanite cube or plane, assign a simple opaque Default Lit material, and add a movable point light. Give the material a recognizable Base Color, a constant Roughness, and no world-position offset. In the viewport's View Mode menu, open Buffer Visualization and inspect Base Color, World Normal, Roughness, and Scene Depth one at a time. The exact labels are registered in the engine visualization configuration. These modes expose different intermediate values at the same visible surface rather than four alternative final looks.

Move the point light while keeping the object and camera fixed. The Lit result should change as illumination changes; the simple material's Base Color and Roughness should not change merely because the light moved. Rotate the object instead, and the World Normal view should change orientation. Then use viewmode wireframe on this conventional mesh to inspect its edges and viewmode lit to return. These commands are documented in Viewport Modes. The experiment gives a practical debugging fork: incorrect Base Color points toward material inputs; correct surface data with unexpected Lit output points toward lighting, visibility, or later processing.

For a bounds check, enable Show → Advanced → Bounds in the editor viewport and inspect the object while changing a deformation or its advertised bounds. Bounds is a registered advanced show flag. A visible surface outside its bound is a correctness warning; a very large bound enclosing a small surface explains why culling may be ineffective. This is an observation exercise rather than a demand to reduce every bound aggressively: the bound must still enclose the geometry in all supported poses.

13Separate the room's surfaces from the light they reflect

The same seven components produce several useful per-pixel descriptions. First examine base color. It answers what material property the winning surface supplies, before indirect illumination makes the neutral floor appear tinted. The red wall's material and the red light reflected onto the floor are different quantities. The floor keeps its neutral base color even where its final lit appearance becomes red. This is the concrete reason deferred rendering separates surface evaluation from lighting evaluation.

The world-normal view answers a different question: which way does the visible surface face? Identical materials on the floor and back wall do not imply identical illumination, because their normals differ. Under nonuniform scale, transform normals with the inverse transpose of the linear transform and normalize them. The derivation follows from perpendicularity. For a tangent vvv, nTv=0n^Tv=0nTv=0. After transforming the tangent to AvAvAv, choose n′=A−Tnn'=A^{-T}nn′=A−Tn, giving (n′)TAv=nTv=0(n')^TAv=n^Tv=0(n′)TAv=nTv=0. Multiplying a normal by AAA as if it were a position does not preserve this relation for general nonuniform scale.

The matte block uses roughness 0.7 and metallic 0; the glossy block uses roughness 0.12 and metallic 0.85. Roughness changes the distribution of reflection directions, while metallic changes how base color and reflectance participate in the shading model. These values are shader inputs, not labels such as “reflective object” stored on the actor. A low-roughness surface requires sharper directional information from the reflection system than a rough diffuse surface does.

These views are selections of shading inputs, not an exhaustive description of the engine's packed GBuffer layout. The layout can depend on material features and renderer settings. What survives those implementation choices is the contract: visible-surface evaluation makes material properties available, and lighting uses them with positions, normals, light data, shadows, and indirect-light estimates. The light component is not another material slot on each wall. It contributes illumination to relevant receivers through renderer light data and lighting passes.

The ceiling light in this capture is a movable RectLightComponent with 2,400 lumens, source width 130 cm, source height 120 cm, and attenuation radius 2,000 cm. It is placed at (0,270,298) cm and points downward. Exposure is held fixed for the capture sequence. These settings make the experiment reproducible, but the image is not a radiometric comparison with the CPU lab: the reduced renderer uses its own normalized radiance units, while Unreal applies its light-unit conventions, shading, reconstruction, exposure, and display pipeline.

14The camera does not see the whole lighting problem

The lamp lights the slab directly. The slab also receives light that first struck the courtyard's red wall. That second contribution is indirect illumination: the direction and color of arriving light depend on other surfaces. A shiny brass handle reflects a part of the courtyard outside the camera's view. Both effects ask questions that the nearest visible surface at each screen pixel cannot fully answer. This is where the persistent scene and the GBuffer must be kept conceptually separate. The GBuffer describes what this camera currently sees; the scene describes the world that other visibility and lighting queries may need.

A screen-space trace can search depth and other buffers to find a candidate intersection along a projected ray. It is attractive because those buffers already exist and match the visible rasterized geometry closely. But if the red wall is outside the image, its samples are absent. The same problem occurs for surfaces hidden behind the first depth layer. A purely screen-space method cannot recover information that was never stored. Temporal reuse can improve stability and coverage over time, but it does not turn one current image into a complete three-dimensional world.

Hardware ray tracing uses acceleration structures to make three-dimensional intersection queries efficient. A bottom-level acceleration structure, or BLAS, organizes the geometry of an object or geometry group. A top-level acceleration structure, or TLAS, organizes placed instances with their transforms. This resembles the asset-versus-placement distinction with which we began, now specialized for ray traversal. Moving a rigid gate can change an instance transform while reusing its local geometry structure. Deforming a character can require updating or rebuilding geometry data as well. Unreal's ray-tracing scene implementation manages instance data and top-level builds in RayTracingScene.cpp.

A ray intersection is only part of a lighting answer. It tells us that a ray met some geometry at a distance, with information identifying the hit. We still need a surface response and an estimate of illumination at that location. Evaluating the full original material and tracing enough additional rays for every query can be too expensive for a real-time budget. A lighting system therefore chooses representations and caches appropriate to the question. This does not make the cached answer identical to the full path-traced solution; it makes the approximation explicit and affordable.

Lumen uses a combination of tracing and lighting representations. Depending on configuration, it can combine screen traces with software tracing through distance-field representations or hardware ray tracing. A signed distance field stores an estimate of distance to a surface throughout space, allowing a ray to advance according to distance estimates instead of testing all triangles. This representation has its own resolution and shape limitations. Hardware tracing addresses a different geometry representation and has its own update costs. Neither path should be described as “just read the GBuffer for everything.” Epic's Lumen Technical Details explains the configurable tracing paths and their limitations.

Lumen's Surface Cache captures material-related surface information using parameterizations associated with mesh cards, then maintains lighting information useful to indirect queries. A card is an oriented capture representation of part of a surface, not a replacement gameplay object and not simply the final camera GBuffer saved forever. Coverage matters: an interior corner or poorly represented region can have different behavior from a simple exterior wall. The renderer must also respond when the object, its material, or the lighting changes. FLumenSceneData maintains specialized scene data alongside the ordinary renderer scene; its declaration is in LumenSceneData.h.

FLumenSceneData: a maintained representation for indirect-lighting queries

The progression is now concrete: a component authors a change, its rendering representation exposes usable state, scene records organize it, and specialized consumers maintain derived data. The tables identify the information at each boundary; the surrounding walkthrough explains why that boundary exists.

Follow one indirect-light sample in the courtyard conceptually. The visible slab provides a position and surface orientation. A lighting algorithm selects an incoming direction to investigate. A trace finds the red wall, perhaps through a representation other than the main-view triangles. A lighting lookup or hit evaluation estimates the radiance returning from that wall. The slab's own response weights the arriving light, and temporal or spatial filtering stabilizes the estimate under the available sample budget. The exact Lumen pipeline is more sophisticated, but each step now has an understandable responsibility: find a surface, know its appearance and illumination, transport a contribution, and control sampling noise.

This is also why “the object is visible” does not establish that it participates correctly in GI. A procedural mesh can be rasterized by a custom proxy without supplying the representation a particular software tracing path needs. A volume or particle effect may use a separate lighting solution. Material displacement can differ from a fallback ray geometry. Nanite can render extremely detailed visible geometry while another consumer uses a selected fallback or supported specialized ray representation. Compatibility must be tested per consumer and configuration. A scene architecture should represent missing capabilities explicitly, not assume that successful main-view rendering proves universal support.

Unreal's static mesh LOD resources themselves reveal the coexistence of representations: alongside sections and mesh resources are references for distance-field data, card-representation data, and ray-tracing geometry. Those fields may be absent when not available. This is strong evidence for a modular design centered on one object identity with several optional derived products. The fields are declared together in StaticMeshResources.h. Sharing identity allows changes to invalidate the right products; separating products allows each algorithm to use a form suited to its work.

Real-time GI also adds temporal lifetimes. A lighting cache may persist longer than one frame, refine incrementally, and be invalidated by movement, material changes, or lighting changes. A new light might produce visible direct illumination before every cached indirect contribution has fully converged. A scene system should expose enough revision information for consumers to make these decisions. The renderer's graph can order this frame's updates, but it cannot invent the semantic fact that a cached wall capture became stale because the material changed. Scene representation must carry that cause to the lighting subsystem.

Test the representation that a lighting query actually uses

In a project already configured to use Lumen, frame a static mesh with an alcove or interior corner and choose View Mode → Lumen → Overview. Compare the visible object with the three diagnostic panels as in the screenshot. Then choose the Surface Cache visualization and look for magenta coverage gaps on surfaces that are visible in Lit mode. The observation narrows the problem to capture coverage; increasing the main-view triangle count alone does not explain or repair it. Investigate the mesh's structure and capture settings, and compare again after the relevant data has rebuilt.

Open the console and enter r.Lumen.Visualize.CardPlacement 1 to show the capture-card arrangement around the mesh; enter the same command with 0 to turn the overlay off. The local source registers this switch in LumenVisualize.cpp. A broad exterior wall and a deep recess can have very different coverage even when both look perfectly detailed in the normal camera. Inspecting the cards connects an artifact to the particular approximation that produced it.

A second controlled test separates screen information from other tracing data. First query r.Lumen.ScreenProbeGather.ScreenTraces in the console and note its existing value. Temporarily set it to 0, keep the camera and lighting fixed, and compare diffuse indirect illumination; then restore the recorded value. The switch controls screen tracing in screen-probe gathering, not every reflection or shadow feature. The source describes the screen-trace-to-fallback ordering. A change can reveal that screen-visible geometry was supplying information that the fallback representation handles differently. It does not, by itself, prove which fallback product is wrong; it tells you which representation boundary to investigate next.

15Change one room and follow the representations that must respond

Move the matte block while keeping its mesh and material. The capture script changes its mobility to movable and translates it by (−100,−80,0) cm. Its center moves from (77.5,285,52.5) to (−22.5,205,52.5). There is still one shared cube asset and the same material binding. Placement, bounds, visibility, shadows, tracing instances and affected lighting history must respond. This is why “the mesh changed” is an insufficient update message.

Now change only the light's intensity and color, leaving the moved block in place. The light becomes 7,200 lumens with linear RGB (1,0.55,0.25). The cube geometry and material base colors remain unchanged. Direct lighting changes immediately when the new light data is consumed; indirect illumination and histories need their own update policies. A material recapture is not inherently required merely because a light changed. Cached illumination is the affected quantity.

Return to the original room's tracing and caching views. Lumen's mesh distance fields describe geometric proximity for software tracing. Its cards parameterize surfaces for material and lighting storage. These two views answer different questions about the same seven components. A card is not a triangle acceleration structure. A distance field is not a material texture. A valid component transform must place both consistently, but their resolution, update mechanism, and failure modes differ.

This room connects the full architecture. Authoring objects provide semantic identity and editable values. Proxies and scene info organize renderer-owned behavior and membership. GPU records provide compact placement and material access. View passes resolve surfaces. Deferred shading consumes their properties. Lumen maintains additional geometry and radiance representations so light can arrive from surfaces beyond the camera's first hit. The independent Lumen walkthrough follows those caches numerically and visually; the present lesson is that a scene architecture must let each consumer maintain its own representation without losing track of which object and revision it describes.

The reproducibility bundle contains the room creation script, a small project-local editor bridge for verified viewport modes, engine configuration, exported scene inventory, capture commands, and image hashes. Internal proxy addresses, primitive packed indices and draw counts were not instrumented in this experiment, so the essay does not infer them from actor labels. For a future Arda implementation, expose these identities explicitly with generations and revision numbers. That would allow a trace to follow this very block from authoring edit to upload, draw, tracing update and lighting invalidation without relying on a screenshot to guess the transition.

16Deriving an Arda scene from the courtyard

We can now design Arda's future scene layer from concrete obligations. The following is a proposal, not a description of existing Arda classes or a promise to reproduce Unreal's internal architecture verbatim. The courtyard requires shared geometry, individually addressable placements, explicit appearance bindings, safe publication across execution boundaries, efficient GPU data, and several consumers of the same world. It also requires some consumers to use different representations. Those requirements are more durable than the exact names or allocation strategies of a particular engine version.

Begin with durable asset records. A geometry asset owns or refers to source geometry and its derived products. The conventional triangle product might contain vertex streams, indices, section-to-material-slot mapping, LODs, and local bounds. A future virtualized product might contain cluster pages and hierarchy data. A ray product might contain acceleration-structure inputs and build state. A volume product would have a different schema. These products should identify their source revision so a rebuild can be recognized and published without silently mixing new indices with old vertices. Asset identity should survive replacement of its current GPU allocation.

Next define a placed-object record. It references a geometry asset and material bindings, carries current and previous transforms, publishes conservative bounds, and identifies optional deformation or per-instance data. Use a handle with an index and generation at the public scene boundary. Internally, the renderer can map that handle to dense arrays and GPU allocations. The mapping is a renderer responsibility. Gameplay should never need to know whether a placement currently occupies GPU entry 400, because relocation and compaction must remain available optimizations.

A material binding should reference a compiled program plus the resources and parameters it needs. A geometry section selects a binding through a defined slot or index. Per-instance variation should have an explicit format, so the shader can distinguish a transform, an object-level tint, and a particle attribute. The compiled material describes relevant capabilities: opaque or masked coverage, displacement requirements, supported shading representation, and the domains in which it can run. This permits the renderer to reject an unsupported combination with a useful explanation rather than produce an accidental partial result.

Publish changes through typed scene operations. A transform update carries the new transform, bounds, and history policy. A parameter update carries a binding revision. A geometry replacement identifies a new asset product. A removal retires the public handle and schedules reclamation for the appropriate consumers. Collecting these operations into a scene revision gives the renderer a coherent publication boundary. It also permits coalescing: if gameplay moves the gate three times before publication, the renderer may need only the final state plus a correctly defined previous observation.

// Proposed semantic records; these are not existing Arda APIs.
SceneHandle gate = { index: 42, generation: 7 };

TransformUpdate {
    object: gate,
    current: gateToWorldAtFrame121,
    bounds: conservativeGateBoundsAtFrame121,
    history: ContinuousMotion
}

RemoveObject { object: gate }
// A later replacement may use {42, 8}; stale {42, 7} updates fail.

The rendering scene consumes those operations and owns its read-mostly representation. It tracks which GPU records need uploading, which cached commands need rebuilding, which ray structures need updates, and which lighting representations need invalidation. These should be separate dependency consequences, not one undifferentiated “dirty” flag. A transform can update instance data and a TLAS entry. A topology edit can rebuild geometry-related resources. A roughness parameter can invalidate appropriate material or surface-cache state without forcing a new index buffer. Explicit causes keep both correctness and cost visible.

Geometry extensions should supply capabilities through interfaces with narrow responsibilities. A raster provider describes draw or compute-raster inputs. A deformation provider declares input resources, output resources, bounds policy, and history behavior. A ray provider exposes supported geometry and update requirements. An indirect-lighting provider can supply a surface capture or another representation when appropriate. These need not become four virtual methods on every object. They can be registered product types and handlers keyed by geometry kind. The essential requirement is that the core scene can discover and schedule them without knowing every specialized implementation in advance.

The shared GPU scene schema should start with only data broadly required for addressing, transforms, bounds, and flags. Optional payload ranges can hold specialized values. Otherwise each new geometry type will enlarge every object's record, increasing bandwidth for consumers that do not need those fields. Version the CPU-to-shader packing contract and test it with known records. A test object translated by exactly ten units, with a deliberately asymmetric scale and a distinctive instance color, can reveal swapped indices and matrix conventions more effectively than a complicated beauty scene.

A point provider exposes the value of explicit capabilities

Test the proposed design with a deliberately incomplete new feature: a point-cloud provider for the scanned courtyard. Its records contain positions and colors. It can generate camera-facing point footprints for the main raster view, but it has no UV coordinates, no authored surface normals, and no ray-intersection product. A flat vertex-color material is compatible with that declared raster interface. A stone material that requires UV0 and a tangent-space normal map is not. Arda should reject that binding with the missing attributes named, or require an explicitly selected adapter that generates UVs and a documented normal convention. Silently feeding zeros would turn an interface mismatch into an unexplained visual artifact.

The same provider must report its ray capability as unavailable. A successful raster screenshot must not register an imaginary BLAS, promise an accurate mirror reflection, or imply complete GI participation. A later provider could generate triangles or finite ray-intersectable point geometry as a separate product, with explicit quality and update costs. A screen-space effect might still observe the visible footprints, but that observation disappears outside the image and is not equivalent to a persistent world-space tracing representation.

Now edit one scanned point. Its position update dirties the point buffer and conservative bounds, and it changes the raster representation that reads them. If a reconstructed triangle or ray product exists and depends on those samples, its source revision becomes stale and its owner schedules the appropriate update or rebuild. If no such product exists, there is nothing to pretend to update. Old in-flight draws keep the old buffer alive until their consumers finish; the newly published scene revision uses the replacement allocation. Changing only the point's display color can take a narrower path, provided no declared derived product uses that color. This is a small, testable extension of the scene's identity, dependency, and lifetime rules.

Keep persistent scene state distinct from frame work. The scene owns object identity, resource references, revisions, and temporal state. A frame builds views and schedules uploads, deformation, visibility, rasterization, lighting, and image processing through a graph of resource dependencies. Transient depth or GBuffer textures belong to that frame's rendering work; the slab asset does not disappear when those textures are recycled. Persistent lighting caches span frames but are owned by their subsystem and keyed to scene revisions. This separation gives a render graph useful freedom without making it the database of the world.

Streaming follows the same rule. A geometry asset can exist before its preferred LOD or cluster page is resident. The scene record remains valid while a resource manager selects a resident fallback or delays a particular consumer. Residency is not the same thing as object existence. Different consumers can require different products: a far object may need a coarse visible mesh, an occlusion representation, or a ray-tracing fallback. Making residency state explicit prevents one missing high-detail page from becoming a dangling scene reference.

Now run one complete frame. Gameplay advances the gate hinge and the character pose, spawns new fountain particles, and changes the lamp intensity. It publishes a coherent batch of scene operations. The render scene resolves handles, updates world-space records and conservative bounds, and records affected representations. GPU uploads make changed primitive and instance data available. Deformation produces the character's current surface and the history needed for motion. View-dependent culling selects work for the camera and other consumers without destroying off-screen objects.

The raster path combines geometry access, material behavior, and pass requirements. Opaque and masked surfaces produce depth and the chosen deferred surface representation. Shadow work establishes relevant light visibility. Direct lighting evaluates the lamp against those surface properties. Indirect lighting queries the representations it supports, uses or refreshes persistent caches, and contributes reflected illumination. Transparent spray, hair, and mist follow their declared specialized paths and are composed into the image. Temporal and post-processing consumers use motion, history validity, depth, and color to produce the final display image.

At the end of that frame, several forms of the courtyard still coexist. Gameplay retains actors and component relationships. The renderer retains registered objects and their render products. GPU buffers retain addressable scene records. Acceleration structures retain a form suited to rays. Lighting caches retain partial answers worth reusing. None is the universal master layout for every subsystem. They remain coherent because identity, publication, dependency, and lifetime have explicit contracts.

That is the essential structure of scene representation. A triangle became a shared asset; a placement gave it identity; a component made it authorable; a proxy made parallel rendering safe; GPU records made it efficiently addressable; pass processing made it usable by different raster operations; and additional representations made it visible to lighting queries beyond the camera. Arda can begin with a modest triangle renderer while preserving these boundaries. The value of the design is that adding a terrain patch, a simulated ribbon, or a new GI method then extends known contracts instead of forcing every system to agree on one increasingly overloaded kind of scene node.

17The geometry compatibility contract Arda needs

“Load an Unreal scene” needs a more precise promise than “support meshes.” A courtyard can contain a conventional stone mesh, Nanite architecture, instanced grass, a skinned character, a spline road, particles, hair, water, fog, and a world-space interface. They can all contribute to one image, but they do not share one raw data format or one rendering path. The following illustrated inventory defines a proposed Arda compatibility contract. It does not claim these adapters already exist in Arda.

The scope is the rendering families present in the inspected Unreal 5.8.1 source, including named optional plugins. Baseline identifies the core scene-adapter targets proposed here; feature mode adds a distinct evaluation or representation; plugin scope requires the corresponding plugin's assets and semantics. These are implementation-planning labels, not statements that a plugin's visuals are unimportant. A project claiming compatibility with content using one of these families must implement it or report the unsupported feature explicitly. Unreal permits additional plugins and custom components, so no finite built-in list guarantees arbitrary-project compatibility.

Each illustration below is an original schematic of the geometry or visible effect, not an Unreal screenshot. The diagrams make differences in representation visible: repeated instances, skinned surfaces, centerline-expanded ribbons, sampled points, and integrated volume density should not all be imagined as interchangeable static meshes. A file extension such as FBX, Alembic, USD, LAS, or VDB describes an import path; it does not by itself define the runtime primitive or its renderer.

1. Conventional static meshes

Baseline · UStaticMeshComponent. The asset supplies indexed triangle sections, vertex attributes, material slots, bounds, and conventional LOD resources; the component supplies placement and rendering flags. Arda needs an adapter that preserves section/material identity, UV and tangent conventions, current and previous transforms, LOD selection, and culling bounds. It must then provide the appropriate depth, base, shadow, and velocity work. Ray-tracing geometry and distance-field or card representations are additional products, not fields that magically appear because the raster mesh loaded. Material blending and World Position Offset can change which passes are needed. A rigid object moving every frame still belongs to this geometry family; “static mesh” describes its asset representation, not an immovable actor. StaticMeshComponent.h

2. Nanite-enabled triangle geometry

Feature mode · typically UStaticMeshComponent, also the supported instanced, spline, skinned, and collection paths. Supporting a conventional static mesh does not mean Arda can consume Nanite's cluster hierarchy, streaming pages, visibility results, or programmable raster/shading behavior. Arda must either implement a compatible virtualized-geometry representation or explicitly select an available conventional fallback with a stated fidelity difference. Displacement, masking, deformation, shadow rendering, and ray tracing each need their own capability decision. An acceleration structure may use a fallback or another supported Nanite representation; it is not automatically the same triangles selected for the camera. The inspected code has a separate skinned-Nanite gate, so the common claim that Nanite categorically means rigid static geometry is already too narrow for this revision. SkinnedMeshComponent.cpp: Nanite feature gate See also Epic's versioned Nanite overview.

3. ISM, HISM, foliage, and landscape grass

Baseline, with feature modes · UInstancedStaticMeshComponent, UHierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponent, UFoliageInstancedStaticMeshComponent, and UGrassInstancedStaticMeshComponent. The raw surface is shared; instance transforms, previous transforms, custom data, visibility, and identifiers vary. HISM adds hierarchical organization, while foliage and grass systems own placement and regeneration policies. Arda needs stable instance identity, bulk updates, per-instance data, culling/LOD behavior, and material access to instance variation. Expanding all instances into unrelated duplicated meshes can reproduce a picture but loses the memory, update, and GPU-driven behavior needed at foliage scale. A supported Nanite mesh changes the geometry backend, not the ownership of instance data. Shadow and ray representations must preserve the relevant instances, and masked or displaced vegetation needs consistent bounds and coverage. InstancedStaticMeshComponent.h HierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponent.h FoliageInstancedStaticMeshComponent.h GrassInstancedStaticMeshComponent.h

4. Skinned meshes, morphs, cloth, and mesh deformers

Baseline skinning plus feature modes · USkeletalMeshComponent through USkinnedMeshComponent. Inputs include indexed geometry, bone indices and weights, a pose, optional morph deltas, cloth output, and mesh-deformer results. Arda's adapter must define the deformation order and provide current and previous deformed positions, shading attributes, material sections, and updated bounds. A bind-pose mesh plus an actor transform is insufficient. Velocity and shadow passes need compatible deformation; ray-tracing geometry needs an appropriate build or update, and GI representations can have different fidelity or update cadence. Nanite skinning is separately gated in this checkout and does not prove that every morph, cloth, or deformer combination follows that path. Record the specific supported combination and fallback rather than advertising one Boolean “skeletal support.” SkeletalMeshComponent.h SkinnedMeshComponent.cpp: skinned rendering modes

The adapter should target the skinned/deformation contract rather than recognize only USkeletalMeshComponent. UPoseableMeshComponent supplies manually controlled poses. UInstancedSkinnedMeshComponent adds instance transforms, animation indices, custom data, and previous transforms, so instancing is not limited to static meshes. In the Chaos Cloth Asset plugin, UChaosClothComponent also derives from USkinnedMeshComponent and accepts cloth or outfit assets. Each producer needs its appropriate pose/deformation handoff; none is correctly covered by checking only the skeletal-component class name. PoseableMeshComponent.h InstancedSkinnedMeshComponent.h Chaos ClothAsset/ClothComponent.h

5. Landscape heightfields and Nanite Landscape

Baseline terrain plus feature mode · ULandscapeComponent and ULandscapeNaniteComponent. Conventional Landscape uses tiled height and weight data, terrain topology/LOD rules, material layers, and hole information. Arda must preserve tile adjacency, coordinate/scale conventions, layer sampling, holes, bounds, and a compatible terrain surface. Nanite Landscape adds derived Nanite mesh data through a distinct component type. It does not make every heightfield use disappear: collision, water-related use, and other systems can still depend on the original terrain representation. Shadows and GI must consume a representation with the same shape and holes; a generic flat grid with a color texture is not terrain compatibility. The two component classes and Epic's Nanite Landscape documentation make the coexistence explicit. LandscapeComponent.h LandscapeNaniteComponent.h

A separate plugin provider, UVirtualHeightfieldMeshComponent, renders a heightfield from a Runtime Virtual Texture heightmap. It is not a renamed ULandscapeComponent. Arda needs the virtual-texture producer and sampling contract, min/max height data, tile/LOD selection, material binding, and the provider's explicit velocity/shadow capabilities. The lower panel above illustrates this alternative data source. A static export of the resulting surface is a possible approximation, but it loses live updates to the virtual height field. VirtualHeightfieldMeshComponent.h

6. Spline-deformed meshes and spline data

Feature mode · USplineMeshComponent; distinguish USplineComponent. A spline mesh deforms a source static mesh using spline parameters, roll, scale, and an axis convention. Arda must evaluate compatible positions and tangents, expand conservative bounds, and retain prior deformation for motion when needed. A spline component stores curve information and can draw a debug visualization, but it does not inherently generate a production road or cable surface. It actually derives from UPrimitiveComponent in this source; inheritance alone therefore cannot be used to infer a production geometry contract. Its debug draw relevance is gated by spline visualization settings. Conventional or Nanite spline rendering, shadows, ray geometry, and Lumen capture each require consistent deformation or an explicit approximation. SplineMeshComponent.h SplineComponent.h SplineComponent.cpp: debug draw relevance

7. Procedural mesh sections

Plugin scope · UProceduralMeshComponent. Its section-creation API accepts vertex positions, triangle indices, normals, UV sets, colors, and tangents. Arda needs a section-based mutable mesh adapter with validated indices, material assignment, explicit update lifetimes, and bounds recomputation. Collision creation is a separate request in the API; a collision mesh is not a substitute for the rendering buffers. Position-only updates and topology replacements should invalidate different resources where possible. Conventional raster, depth, shadow, velocity, and optional ray geometry need compatible updates; prebuilt static-mesh distance fields or Nanite pages should not be assumed to exist for arbitrary newly generated triangles. This family is about application-provided geometry, not any particular algorithm used to generate it. ProceduralMeshComponent.h: section data contract

8. Editable dynamic meshes

Feature mode · UDynamicMeshComponent through UBaseDynamicMeshComponent. The source representation is FDynamicMesh3 through a mesh object, with attributes and potentially changing topology. Arda must convert or directly maintain compatible render sections, attribute seams, material IDs, and update regions. Unreal exposes different notifications for full mesh changes and more limited attribute or position changes, demonstrating why a single “upload mesh again” operation misses useful update semantics. A runtime cut can invalidate index buffers, bounds, acceleration structures, and secondary surface representations together. Raster support alone does not establish automatic Nanite, distance-field, or GI-cache support for every edit; each representation needs an explicit rebuild/update policy. DynamicMeshComponent.h: mesh representation DynamicMeshComponent.h: update notifications

9. Geometry-cache animation

Plugin scope · UGeometryCacheComponent. Geometry caches provide time-sampled mesh tracks, transforms, bounds, and applicable motion information; topology can differ according to the cache content and codec. Arda's adapter needs track/time selection, interpolation rules where supported, sample streaming, materials, and previous-position or motion-vector semantics. Treating every sample as a skeletal pose invents a bone model the asset does not contain. Conversely, displaying only one frame loses the essential behavior. Shadows and ray-tracing geometry must update with the chosen sample, and expensive rebuilds or missing secondary GI representations must be reported as capability limits. Alembic is a possible content route into such a cache, not the runtime component itself. GeometryCacheComponent.h: track-oriented component GeometryCacheComponent.h: motion-vector controls

10. Chaos Geometry Collections

Feature mode · UGeometryCollectionComponent. A collection carries mesh pieces, a transform hierarchy, material assignments, and simulation-driven visibility or fracture state. Arda needs piece identity and transforms, the relationship between parent clusters and visible pieces, interior-face materials, bounds, and current/previous state. A single combined triangle mesh may reproduce the intact object but cannot reproduce the transition to independently moving fragments without additional structure. Conventional and Nanite collection rendering are separate supported modes to negotiate. Shadow and ray representations must follow active pieces; secondary lighting representations may update at a different rate. Chaos simulation itself can remain a distinct producer of state if the compatibility goal is rendering its output, but the rendered result must preserve the simulation's piece activation and motion. GeometryCollectionComponent.h

11. BSP/model surfaces and brush visualization

Feature mode · UModelComponent; distinguish UBrushComponent. Older or blockout-oriented levels can contain model surfaces derived from BSP/brush operations. Arda needs the resulting polygon/triangle surfaces, surface material assignments, texture-coordinate mapping, bounds, and visibility semantics if these levels are in scope. It need not execute the editor's entire constructive modeling workflow merely to render a cooked result. A brush component can also serve editor or volume visualization, so copying its displayed wireframe is not necessarily the intended production surface. Conventional raster compatibility should be assessed separately from ray tracing, Nanite conversion, and GI data; converting a model to a supported static mesh is an explicit migration path with its own fidelity checks. ModelComponent.h BrushComponent.h

12. Niagara and Cascade sprite particles

Plugin scope · UNiagaraComponent with UNiagaraSpriteRendererProperties. Input records carry positions, sizes, rotations, colors, velocities, and material attributes produced by CPU or GPU simulation. Arda needs compatible particle-buffer bindings, billboard orientation, sorting and bounds, indirect counts where applicable, and the renderer's material-input convention. A particle is not a separate UObject mesh component. Translucent sprites need their appropriate compositing and lighting path; masked sprites have different coverage/shadow behavior. Motion, shadow casting, ray visibility, and participation in GI are renderer/material features to negotiate, not consequences of drawing a quad. Matching the simulation output format and sprite expansion is the rendering contract even if the simulation implementation lives elsewhere. NiagaraComponent.h NiagaraSpriteRendererProperties.h

Legacy Cascade content uses UParticleSystemComponent and its emitter/module data instead of Niagara. Its sprite output has a similar low-level quad form but different simulation, attribute, and sorting conventions, so it requires a separate source adapter. The same distinction applies to its mesh, beam, and ribbon modes described below. Supporting Niagara does not automatically import Cascade assets. ParticleSystemComponent.h ParticleModuleRequired.h

13. Niagara and Cascade ribbons and beams

Plugin scope · UNiagaraComponent with UNiagaraRibbonRendererProperties. A ribbon uses ordered points, ribbon identifiers, width, tangent/facing data, tessellation, and UV-distribution rules to construct connected surface geometry. Beam templates can use this machinery with an appropriate point-generation arrangement; do not invent a required UNiagaraBeamRendererProperties class. Arda needs ordering, connectivity, width expansion, interpolation, materials, bounds, and previous-frame behavior. Independent point sprites cannot reproduce a continuous ribbon's silhouette or texture flow. Sorting, translucency, shadow behavior, and ray/GI representation remain separate choices, particularly when a rapidly changing trail's topology or length changes every frame. NiagaraRibbonRendererProperties.h

For legacy Cascade, the exact source modes include UParticleModuleTypeDataRibbon and UParticleModuleTypeDataBeam2 within UParticleSystemComponent. Their tessellation, connectivity, and material-coordinate conventions must be translated explicitly. Unlike the Niagara example above, a named Beam2 type-data class does exist here. The shared graphical forms explain what can be reused in Arda's renderer; they do not erase the producer-specific contract. ParticleModuleTypeDataRibbon.h ParticleModuleTypeDataBeam2.h

14. Niagara and Cascade mesh particles

Plugin scope · UNiagaraComponent with UNiagaraMeshRendererProperties. Mesh particles combine particle attributes with selected mesh resources, material overrides, and renderer-specific scaling/orientation. Arda can reuse mesh and instance machinery, but it must adapt particle-driven counts, selection, bounds, previous transforms, and simulation-buffer ownership. The instanced data source and lifetime differ from a persistent ISM component. Conventional, Nanite-related plugin paths, shadows, and ray visibility must be identified separately for the selected renderer and platform. A generic “Niagara supported” label that handles only sprites would silently lose debris meshes; a mesh-only implementation would lose smoke and trails. These three particle entries are distinct renderer modes under the same high-level component. NiagaraMeshRendererProperties.h

Cascade's UParticleModuleTypeDataMesh is the legacy mesh-particle producer and likewise needs its own attribute adapter. Niagara also has renderer families beyond the three surface forms illustrated here: UNiagaraVolumeRendererProperties connects to heterogeneous volume rendering, while UNiagaraLightRendererProperties and UNiagaraDecalRendererProperties produce scene-service contributions. Thus the three particle surface entries are not an exhaustive inventory of Niagara renderer outputs. ParticleModuleTypeDataMesh.h NiagaraLightRendererProperties.h NiagaraDecalRendererProperties.h

15. Groom strands, cards, and hair meshes

Plugin scope · UGroomComponent. Strands use curve samples with hair-specific attributes and specialized visibility/shading; cards and meshes use surface geometry approximating groups of hairs. Arda must preserve the selected representation, root binding, deformation/simulation output, LOD transitions, material requirements, and bounds. Treating strand data as an ordinary indexed triangle buffer omits the curve-to-coverage problem and hair scattering. Cards require alpha/coverage and orientation behavior consistent with their textures. Shadows and ray tracing have representation-specific resources, and GI behavior is not established merely by a successful main-view image. The component explicitly carries strand, card, and mesh material/resource concepts; compatibility must state which modes are supported. GroomComponent.h: representation-specific materials

16. LiDAR point clouds

Plugin scope · ULidarPointCloudComponent. Raw points carry positions and appearance data, with spatial organization and point-rendering controls. Arda needs point selection/streaming, size or footprint interpretation, color mapping, camera behavior, and bounds. Rendering a small billboard or splat for each selected point is different from assuming the source contains a watertight triangle mesh. A reconstructed triangle proxy, if generated for another purpose, is a separate representation. Shadow casting, ray intersections, and GI coverage must be implemented or approximated deliberately; gaps between samples and point-size choices change visible coverage. The component exposes point size, shape, orientation, and coloration settings that belong in the adapter contract. LidarPointCloudComponent.h: point appearance controls

17. Sparse heterogeneous volumes: smoke, fire, and fog

Feature mode · UHeterogeneousVolumeComponent, with sparse-volume assets/materials as applicable. Inputs describe spatial fields such as density, scattering, absorption, and emission, potentially animated through Sparse Volume Texture frames. Arda needs volume bounds and transforms, field sampling/streaming, time selection, step/integration policy, volume-domain material evaluation, and appropriate light/shadow interaction. A cube can bound the work, but shading only the cube's faces cannot reproduce the smoke. Ordinary surface GBuffer, triangle BLAS, and card-capture support do not imply volume support. The component's resolution, frame transform, and animation fields expose this different data model; Epic's volume documentation details the renderer-specific path. HeterogeneousVolumeComponent.h

Niagara can also produce this renderer family through UNiagaraVolumeRendererProperties, whose UseHeterogeneousVolumes() returns true. In the inspected header its source mode is Emitter, and particle source mode is explicitly left as future work; this is not evidence that arbitrary per-particle volumes are supported. Arda needs that emitter-level volume's material bindings, transform, size/resolution, and sampling parameters in addition to the volume consumer itself. NiagaraVolumeRendererProperties.h: volume path and source-mode limit

18. Volumetric cloud layers

Feature mode · UVolumetricCloudComponent, which derives from USceneComponent. Cloud layer altitude/height, a volume material, tracing limits, and lighting/shadow settings describe the rendered medium. Arda needs a cloud/atmosphere adapter with compatible density coordinates, ray integration, aerial perspective, temporal treatment, and light interaction. This cannot be discovered solely by enumerating UPrimitiveComponent objects. A sky-textured sphere is an explicitly different approximation. Main-view, reflection, and shadow ray sampling have separate controls in the component, so a single generic triangle-pass capability flag cannot describe cloud compatibility. VolumetricCloudComponent.h: layer and sampling settings

19. Paper2D sprites, flipbooks, and tile maps

Plugin scope · UPaperSpriteComponent, UPaperFlipbookComponent, and UPaperTileMapComponent. Sprites provide planar render geometry and texture regions; flipbooks choose sprite frames over time; tile maps arrange cells into layers with per-tile appearance and transforms. Arda needs pivots, pixel-to-world scale, UV/atlas handling, frame timing, layer ordering, material/blend behavior, and bounds. Flattening a tile map into a photograph loses parallax and editable layer semantics; treating a flipbook as one permanent quad texture loses its animation contract. Depth, shadow, and lighting behavior depend on the chosen materials and renderer settings. These surfaces may share low-level triangle code while still requiring different source adapters. PaperSpriteComponent.h PaperFlipbookComponent.h PaperTileMapComponent.h

20. Billboards and material billboards

Feature mode · UBillboardComponent and UMaterialBillboardComponent. A billboard describes a facing quad or similar generated surface, its texture/material, sizing, and potentially distance-dependent appearance. Arda must reproduce camera-facing orientation, screen/world size interpretation, bounds, and depth/translucency behavior. Do not replace all billboards with fixed world planes: their silhouette changes differently as the camera moves. Some uses are editor icons and should be excluded from a production-scene export according to visibility flags; others are intentional in-game visuals. Shadow, ray, and GI inclusion must follow the content's role and explicit capability, rather than manufacturing solid geometry from every icon. BillboardComponent.h MaterialBillboardComponent.h

21. World-space text

Feature mode · UTextRenderComponent. Text content, font metrics/atlas data, alignment, world scale, color, and material settings determine the generated glyph surfaces. Arda needs compatible text layout and glyph sampling as well as a rendering adapter; loading only the component transform and font texture is insufficient. Text changes can change geometry and bounds. Depth, masking/translucency, and material lighting determine its pass behavior. Ray and GI treatment should be explicitly scoped; a distant label does not automatically need a solid volumetric proxy. This is world-space scene text, distinct from a screen-space UI overlay or arbitrary rich UMG widget composition. TextRenderComponent.h

22. World-space widget surfaces

Feature mode · UWidgetComponent. In world space, the widget is rendered to a target and displayed using a configured geometric surface; the component exposes plane/cylinder geometry modes, draw size, and render-target access. Arda needs either compatible widget evaluation or an explicitly supplied rendered UI surface, then the correct transform, curvature, material, alpha handling, timing, and bounds. Screen-space mode belongs to a different composition path and must not be exported as an arbitrary world quad. Interaction/hit testing is a separate compatibility concern beyond drawing. Shadows and GI depend on the surface/material policy; preserving readable UI usually requires deliberate treatment rather than assuming ordinary lit opaque shading. WidgetComponent.h: spaces and geometry modes WidgetComponent.h: render target and sizing

23. Water bodies and their generated surfaces

Plugin scope · UWaterBodyComponent and the Water plugin's mesh-producing components. Water bodies carry shape, material, and water-specific state and can contribute to the shared water mesh or use alternative primitive/static-mesh components. Arda needs the resulting surface topology/LOD, wave displacement, bounds, materials, depth/underwater semantics, and relevant scene textures. Importing only a river spline does not reproduce its rendered water. Reflection, refraction, shadowing, and GI behavior are specialized material/rendering features to negotiate; a blue opaque mesh is merely an explicit fallback. The source exposes both whether a body affects the water mesh and a list of alternative primitive components, making the description/geometry distinction visible. WaterBodyComponent.h: water mesh and alternative primitives

24. Scene contributors that are not ordinary geometry

Separate scene services · UDecalComponent, ULightComponentBase and derived lights, USkyAtmosphereComponent, and UPostProcessComponent. These derive from USceneComponent in the inspected hierarchy rather than from the ordinary mesh/primitive path. Decals project material effects onto eligible receivers; lights supply illumination; atmosphere supplies participating-medium behavior; post-process components supply view settings. Arda needs corresponding service adapters, receiver/pass rules, and blending/priority semantics. Their gizmos or volume bounds are not the final visual effect. Separately, UShapeComponent descendants such as collision boxes, spheres, and capsules, brush volumes, and spline debug lines can derive from primitive classes while serving collision or visualization. Include them as visible production geometry only when content actually requests that visualization. No automatic shadow/ray/GI mesh should be invented from every editor outline. DecalComponent.h LightComponentBase.h SkyAtmosphereComponent.h PostProcessComponent.h ShapeComponent.h

Fog deserves its own service adapter as well. UExponentialHeightFogComponent describes an exponential height distribution and can enable a distinct volumetric-fog mode; ULocalFogVolumeComponent supplies bounded radial/height extinction and scattering. Both derive from USceneComponent. Neither is equivalent to importing a Sparse Volume Texture into UHeterogeneousVolumeComponent. Arda must preserve density distributions, transforms, lighting/composition rules, and feature settings; a triangle shadow or a Lumen card cannot stand in for participating-medium integration. Niagara light and decal renderer outputs must feed the corresponding services while respecting their simulation/source-mode gates. ExponentialHeightFogComponent.h: base and density ExponentialHeightFogComponent.h: volumetric mode LocalFogVolumeComponent.h

This inventory suggests a practical import result for each component: retain its source family and feature modes, identify the renderable representation, and record which consumers can use it. A mesh can be supported for opaque raster and shadows while its animated ray geometry or GI proxy remains unsupported. A volume can be supported through integration while having no triangle representation at all. Compatibility should therefore be reported as family × feature mode × renderer consumer, with an explicit approximation or rejection for missing combinations.

For Arda, the first implementation milestone can cover indexed meshes, instancing, skinning, and material/transform contracts, while reserving stable interfaces for mutable geometry, curves/particles, volumes, and scene services. That is an implementation order, not permission to silently discard the later families when loading a scene. The importer should report them with component names and concrete unsupported modes. Once the relevant adapters exist, the same shared scene identity and update machinery can feed depth, surface shading, shadows, ray tracing, and GI without pretending that all five consumers need identical geometry.
